lede.headline: Tesla's new Roadster flies on SpaceX thrusters
lede.dek: Musk's long-delayed sports car finally launched off a ramp and landed itself using SpaceX-built thrusters, feeding talk of a bigger deal between his two companies.

top10AsOf: List as of Sep 24, 2026 9:15 PM ET

stories.headline: Tesla's new Roadster flies on SpaceX thrusters
stories.move: Tesla showed its second-generation Roadster on Oct. 15 at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas. In a livestreamed demo, cold-gas thrusters built with SpaceX engineers launched the car off a ramp, flipped it in the air and landed it on its wheels; a second run had it jump over a row of vehicles. Musk said production will begin in 2028, eight years after the car's original 2020 target. Tesla gave no price, taking $50,000 deposits for a Performance version and $250,000 for a Thrust version.
stories.why: The SpaceX-built thrusters and the timing fed analyst speculation that Musk could be building toward merging Tesla and SpaceX.
stories.bear: The car won't ship for two more years, and one analyst estimated volumes of only about 2,000 a year, tiny next to Tesla's regular sales.
stories.watch: Whether Tesla's board raises a Tesla-SpaceX merger at its annual meeting, expected by Dec. 6.

stories.headline: Meta and Apple team up to run AI model on Macs
stories.move: Meta released its Muse Spark Open AI model on Oct. 15 and said it worked with Apple to let the model run locally on two linked Mac Studio computers using Apple's M5 Ultra chips and its MLX software. The model has 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active at a time, and a 1-million-token context window, aimed at coding and multi-step agent tasks. Apple CEO John Ternus said it's 'amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk.'
stories.why: It's an unusual collaboration between two companies with a history of friction over privacy rules, and shows Meta pushing its open model onto more hardware.
stories.bear: The 512GB Mac Studio needed to run it hadn't shipped yet, and the setup needs multiple machines that already cost over $10,000 each, not an ordinary single Mac.
stories.watch: Whether Apple ships the 512GB Mac Studio this month as planned.

stories.headline: Berkshire adds $330 million to Bending Spoons stake
stories.move: Berkshire Hathaway agreed on Oct. 14 to buy 10 million new Bending Spoons shares at $33 each, a $330 million private placement that raises its stake in the Italian software company to about 4%. It follows Berkshire's $600 million investment at Bending Spoons' July 2026 IPO. Bending Spoons said the new capital would support further acquisitions.
stories.why: It shows Buffett still betting on Bending Spoons' acquisition-driven model just three months after its IPO.
stories.bear: Berkshire is concentrating more money in a young, newly public company without the long track record Buffett typically demands before investing.
stories.watch: Any new acquisition Bending Spoons announces with the fresh capital.

stories.headline: Jury finds Arm breached Qualcomm license, awards $2
stories.move: A Delaware federal jury ruled on Oct. 13 that Arm Holdings, majority-owned by Masayoshi Son's SoftBank, breached its architecture license agreement with Qualcomm by withholding software patches and tools, and that Arm intentionally interfered with Qualcomm's relationship with Meta. The jury awarded Qualcomm only $2 in nominal damages and ruled for Arm on five other claims. A separate, potentially larger royalty dispute between the two companies now goes to the judge.
stories.why: It's a narrow, low-dollar win for Qualcomm in a long-running fight that could still affect how much Arm collects in chip-design royalties.
stories.bear: The damages were trivial and the jury rejected most of Qualcomm's other claims, so the practical impact on Arm's business may be limited until the royalty ruling.
stories.watch: Judge Maryellen Noreika's ruling on the remaining royalty dispute.

stories.headline: JPMorgan blocks outside AI agents from accounts
stories.move: On JPMorgan's Oct. 13 third-quarter earnings call, CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank won't let outside AI agents, such as Meta's Muse, log into or act on customer accounts. 'We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company,' he said, adding 'you don't want rogue agents.' A bank spokesperson said JPMorgan blocks third-party agents that try to access accounts using customers' banking credentials. The quarter's results also missed estimates, and Dimon said the bank cut back share buybacks.
stories.why: Banks are racing to let AI agents handle payments, and Dimon is drawing a line at the risk that poses to clients and the bank itself.
stories.bear: The policy could leave JPMorgan behind if rivals let AI agents manage money more freely and customers migrate there.
stories.watch: Whether JPMorgan sets a timeline for its own customer-facing AI agent tools.

stories.headline: Reliance pays staff early ahead of record Jio IPO
stories.move: Ahead of Jio Platforms' IPO, Reliance paid October salaries to its nearly 420,000 group employees about 15 days early and encouraged them to invest, without saying why, according to a Bloomberg report. The IPO's anchor book opens Oct. 19 and public bidding runs Oct. 21-23, targeting up to 30,200 crore rupees (about $3.2 billion) at a price band of 1,065 to 1,119 rupees a share, valuing Jio at up to 10.3 lakh crore rupees (about $108 billion). Up to 500 crore rupees of shares are set aside for eligible Jio employees at a 5% discount.
stories.why: It's one of India's largest-ever IPOs, and the early pay and outreach show how hard Reliance is pushing to build demand beyond big institutional investors.
stories.bear: Encouraging employees to put personal savings into a company-linked stock concentrates their financial risk in one bet.
stories.watch: Jio Platforms' public subscription window, Oct. 21-23.

stories.headline: Michael Dell calls for AI 'guardrails' and oversight
stories.move: In an Oct. 13 CNBC interview, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell said AI models need 'safeguards and controls,' and that companies should limit AI systems to 'bounded permissions' so they can only do what they're explicitly authorized to do. He said government has a role in overseeing AI but declined to propose specific policies, saying that's outside his role as a business leader.
stories.why: A major supplier of the hardware behind the AI buildout is publicly calling for guardrails even as his company profits from that spending.
stories.bear: Calling for government to play 'a role' without specifics leaves the actual policy fight unresolved.
stories.watch: Any specific AI safety framework Dell endorses.

stories.headline: Broadcom's Tan says capital, not chips, limits AI
stories.move: Speaking on a panel in Singapore on Oct. 12, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said capital, not chip or memory shortages, will be the biggest constraint on AI growth, even as Broadcom works through earlier wafer and memory shortfalls. He said demand for AI computing still outpaces supply and could stay that way through 2029 or into 2030, and compared many AI investors to casino gamblers who don't understand what they're buying.
stories.why: One of the biggest AI chip suppliers is warning that funding, not hardware, could be what slows the AI buildout.
stories.bear: Tan has a financial interest in talking up continued AI chip demand even while flagging funding risk elsewhere in the industry.
stories.watch: Whether AI financing costs rise enough to slow data-center spending.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Huang calls AI 'potentially dangerous,' urges talks
stories.move: At a media briefing in London on Oct. 14, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called AI 'potentially dangerous' but said the U.S., U.K. and China should keep talking rather than add new rules, saying 'dialogue, dialogue.' He said he keeps in regular contact with AI researchers in China and wants the U.S. and U.K. to do the same, while telling investors to model Nvidia's China revenue as zero under current export rules.
stories.why: Huang is pushing cooperation over restriction even as U.S. export curbs already keep Nvidia largely out of China's market, a stance that puts him at odds with rivals pushing for tougher AI rules.
stories.bear: Favoring dialogue over regulation also serves Nvidia's commercial interest in keeping access to Chinese research ties open.
stories.watch: Whether the U.S. eases any chip-export restrictions on China.
